1:
The psalm's standing is settled before its sense. Delitzsch reports Luther's answer when asked which were the best psalms, that they were the Pauline ones, this among them, since the condemnability of the natural man, the freeness of mercy and the spiritual nature of redemption are here expressed in a Pauline way; it stands sixth among the seven penitential psalms. Clarke observes that it has no title or author in the Hebrew or any version, though a Syriac tradition assigns it to Nehemiah, and dates it to the captivity.

What the depths are is the first question. Augustine takes Jonah as the pattern, whose voice pierced both waves and beast's belly, then turns it inward: this mortal life is our deep, and those are deepest in it who do not cry from it at all, the man overwhelmed by his sins who laughs when told to pray and argues from his prosperity that God cannot regard human affairs. Gill refuses the literal reading and lists the images the depths stand for, debt and the law's prison, a pit with no water, bondage, but settles on a deep sense of sin. Calvin allows either the psalmist's case or the whole Church, and takes the depths for extreme danger of body or mind. Ellicott notes that the phrase recurs for overwhelming distress and is used of the sea. Spurgeon makes the location the point: the depths silence what they engulf, but prayer lived beneath the floods, and deep places beget deep devotion.

Calvin attacks a use of the psalm rather than a reading, noting that the Roman church recites it for the dead on the strength of taking the deep for purgatory, and objecting that from the time it was so applied it was believed to be of no use to the living. He adds that nothing is harder than for men in deep sorrow to stir their minds to pray, and that though we are cold in prayer while we prosper, we are more stupefied still in adversity.

The third verse is felt by all as the psalm's hinge. Henry notices the double naming of God in so few words and hears a dread of his wrath, drawing three lessons: we cannot plead not guilty; if God were extreme to mark our faults we could neither escape nor bear his hand; and it is of his mercy we are not consumed. Clarke answers with a warning: if every deviation in thought, word and deed were set down, none could stand acquitted, and but for the following verse none could be saved. Gill runs through what marking would involve: a watchful eye, a critical examination, charges laid up sealed for another day. Ellicott alone works the philology: the word rendered mark is the one rendered watch two verses later, so if God watched for men's lapses as a man watches for the dawn, nothing but signal punishment could follow; Job believed God did so watch, and Ellicott remarks how this religious people meet misfortune not with murmuring but with contrition.

The forgiveness that follows divides them at the conjunction and at the purpose. Ellicott corrects the English but to for, taking the ellipse as one Israel felt no need to express, and suggests the article may mean the forgiveness we need. Gill and Henry prefer the rendering propitiation, Henry naming Christ the ransom. Clarke quotes the apostle on the advocate who is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world. On the clause about fear, Henry insists the forgiveness is given not to be presumed upon but that God may be worshipped; Wesley specifies a childlike and not a slavish fear, and calls this mercy the foundation of all religion. Ellicott offers a possibility no one else raises, that the fear may be struck not in the forgiven but in the heathen who see the mercy shown to Israel.
5:
The waiting is described before it is grounded. Clarke gives the word its root sense, the extension of a cord from one point to another: God is one point, the human heart the other, and the cord between them is the earnest believing desire of the soul, which is the active waiting God requires. Ellicott catches the tense, that the Hebrew says the psalmist has been waiting and waits still, and marks the earnestness of the repetition. Henry hears the repetition as a climax proper to a song of ascents, and distinguishes the waiting from its profession, the soul waiting in sincerity and for the Lord himself rather than for relief. Gill lists what is waited for, the light of God's countenance, deliverance, an answer to prayer and eternal happiness, and adds that David may have waited for the coming of Christ as all the saints of that age did.

On the ground of the hope Henry is exact: we must hope only for what God has promised, not for the creatures of our own fancy, and must hope for it because he promised it and not from any opinion of our merit.

The watchers for the morning divide them, and Clarke suspects the text. He reports the Chaldee, which makes them men observing the morning watches in order to offer the oblation, notes that most versions read from the morning to the night watches, and suggests the line may mean from morning watch to morning watch, that is, day and night. Ellicott offers the Levite sentinel whose duty was to signal the first ray of dawn and the hour for the temple rites, while allowing that the figure taken generally, of a sufferer waiting for relief, is striking without it. Wesley gives both in a line, soldiers keeping the night watches or temple priests. Henry works the comparison two ways: the watchers are assured the morning will come, and so is the psalmist that God will return in mercy, since God's covenant is firmer than the ordinances of day and night, which shall end; and they are desirous it should come, as sentinels on the walls are, and those who sit up with the sick. He also records a different rendering, under which the soul hastens to the Lord from the morning guards, meaning daily prayer at the morning sacrifice.

The closing exhortation is read as addressed outward. Ellicott corrects the word order to make it the watchword of faith spoken to the nation. Gill takes the psalmist as passing on what he has found, hope for salvation, remission and eternal life. Clarke fastens on the Hebrew article in both nouns and calls it emphatic: not mercy but that mercy, the fund and essence of it, and not redemption but that abundant redemption. Henry divides the two reasons by the light they come from, mercy discovered by nature and redemption by the gospel, and takes the redemption in three parts: its nature as deliverance from the commanding as well as the condemning power of sin, its riches as a fulness enough for all and for each, and its persons as Israel according to the spirit.

On the last verse the question is how far the promise reaches. Gill notes the redemption was future when the words were spoken but certain, and extends the iniquities to original and actual, secret and open. Clarke refuses to restrict it to Israel in Babylon: every believer may take it to himself. Ellicott presses the emphatic pronoun, he and only he, and argues from a parallel psalm asking redemption from all his troubles that this one asks more, deliverance from sin and not only its consequences, belonging as it does to an age of national contrition. On that ground he says the psalm was prepared to be what it has become, one of the penitential psalms of the world.
